echoes.note: Micaiah's vision of a 'lying spirit' put in the mouths of the prophets gives a scriptural precedent for a deceiving spirit operative in false prophecy. This stands behind John's distinction between the Spirit of God and the spirit of error/deception animating the false prophets.

echoes.text: If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises in your midst you, and he gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or the wonder comes to pass, of which he spoke to you, saying, “Let us go after other gods” (which you have not known) “and let us serve them”; you shall not listen to the words of that prophet, or to that dreamer of dreams; for Yahweh your God is testing you, to know whether you love Yahweh your God with all your heart and with all your soul. […]
echoes.note: The motif that testing exposes whether people love the LORD with whole heart frames the discernment of spirits as covenantal loyalty, faintly underlying John's 'whether they are of God.' Marked faint because John's criterion has shifted to christological confession.

pericopes.text: Beloved, let us love one another, for love is of God; and everyone who loves has been born of God, and knows God. He who doesn’t love doesn’t know God, for God is love. By this God’s love was revealed in us, that God has sent his one and only Son into the world that we might live through him. In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins. Beloved, if God loved us in this way, we also ought to love one another. No one has seen God at any time. If we love one another, God remains in us, and his love has been perfected in us.

echoes.text: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,
echoes.note: The declaration 'God is love' distills the self-revelation of the LORD as abounding in steadfast love (hesed). John's identification of love with God's very being is the climactic theological development of the Sinai name-formula proclaiming the LORD merciful, gracious, and abounding in lovingkindness.

echoes.text: He said, “You cannot see my face, for man may not see me and live.”
echoes.note: 'No one has seen God at any time' echoes the LORD's word to Moses, 'you cannot see my face, for no one can see me and live.' John takes the unseeability of God as a premise and resolves it through mutual love: the invisible God is made manifest when believers love one another.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to you out of the midst of the fire: you heard the voice of words, but you saw no form; you only heard a voice.
echoes.note: At Horeb Israel heard a voice but saw no form, reinforcing the unseeability of God that John presupposes in 'no one has seen God at any time.' The Deuteronomic insistence that no visible form accompanied the theophany feeds the Johannine claim that God is known not by sight but by abiding love.

echoes.text: Jacob called the name of the place Peniel: for, he said, “I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved.”
echoes.note: Jacob's wonder at Peniel, 'I have seen God face to face, and yet my life is preserved,' is the counter-instance that John's absolute 'no one has seen God' engages and qualifies. The tradition of the perilous, near-impossible vision of God lies behind John's denial of any direct sight of God.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses, after the death of the two sons of Aaron, when they drew near before Yahweh, and died; and Yahweh said to Moses, “Tell Aaron your brother, not to come at all times into the Most Holy Place within the veil, before the mercy seat which is on the ark; lest he die: for I will appear in the cloud on the mercy seat. “Aaron shall come into the sanctuary with a young bull for a sin offering, and a ram for a burnt offering. He shall put on […]
echoes.note: The sending of the Son 'as the atoning sacrifice (propitiation) for our sins' draws on the Day of Atonement ritual, where the blood of the sin offering and the scapegoat effect expiation before the LORD at the mercy seat (hilasterion). John casts Christ as the means of atonement fulfilling the Levitical kapporet.

echoes.text: Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all. He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t […]
echoes.note: God sending his Son as the atoning sacrifice 'for our sins' echoes the Servant who bore our griefs and was made an offering for sin, the righteous one making many righteous. The vicarious, sin-bearing logic of the Servant Song informs John's account of love defined by the Son sent as propitiation.

echoes.text: Yahweh didn’t set his love on you, nor choose you, because you were more in number than any people; for you were the fewest of all peoples: but because Yahweh loves you, and because he desires to keep the oath which he swore to your fathers, Yahweh has brought you out with a mighty hand, and redeemed you out of the house of bondage, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt.
echoes.note: 'Not that we loved God, but that he loved us' restates the Deuteronomic ground of election: the LORD set his love on Israel not for any merit but because he loved them. The priority and gratuity of divine love that precedes any human response shapes John's theology of love originating wholly in God.

echoes.text: “When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt. They called to them, so they went from them. They sacrificed to the Baals, and burned incense to engraved images. Yet I taught Ephraim to walk. I took them by his arms; but they didn’t know that I healed them. I drew them with cords of a man, with ties of love; and I was to them like those who lift up the yoke on their necks; and I bent down to him and I fed him.
echoes.note: Hosea's portrait of God's parental love drawing Israel with cords of human kindness and bands of love grounds John's claim that love is of God and that God first loved us. The tender, initiating love of the LORD for his child stands behind the manifestation of God's love in sending the Son.

echoes.text: Yahweh appeared of old to me, saying, Yes, I have loved you with an everlasting love: therefore with loving kindness have I drawn you.
echoes.note: 'I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore with lovingkindness have I drawn you' parallels John's account of love revealed and originating in God. The everlasting, drawing love of the LORD in Jeremiah anticipates the divine love manifested in the sending of the Son.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Let us love one another' rests on the Holiness Code command to love your neighbor as yourself. John universalizes and intensifies the neighbor-love command, grounding mutual love in the divine nature itself.

echoes.text: For you love all things that are, And abhor none of the things which you did make; For never would you have formed anything if you did hate it.
echoes.note: 'You love all things that exist... for you would not have made anything if you had hated it' offers a deuterocanonical precedent for predicating love of God's very relation to creation. This anticipates John's bolder 'God is love.'

pericopes.text: By this we know that we remain in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit. We have seen and testify that the Father has sent the Son as the Savior of the world. Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him, and he in God. We know and have believed the love which God has for us. God is love, and he who remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit.
echoes.note: 'Because he has given us of his Spirit' echoes the promise that God will pour out his Spirit on all flesh as the sign of his abiding presence in the last days. John reads the gift of the Spirit as evidence that believers remain in God and God in them.

echoes.text: I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.
echoes.note: 'I will put my Spirit within you and cause you to walk in my statutes' grounds John's claim that we know we abide in God 'because he has given us of his Spirit.' The indwelling Spirit as token of covenant intimacy underlies the Johannine mutual-abiding language.

echoes.text: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,
echoes.note: The summary confession 'God is love' (repeated) again distills the LORD's self-naming as abounding in steadfast love. John makes the Sinai attribute the definitive predicate of the divine being in which the believer abides.

echoes.text: “You are my witnesses,” says Yahweh, “With my servant whom I have chosen; that you may know and believe me, and understand that I am he. Before me there was no God formed, neither will there be after me. I myself am Yahweh; and besides me there is no savior. I have declared, I have saved, and I have shown; and there was no strange god among you. Therefore you are my witnesses”, says Yahweh, “and I am God.
echoes.note: 'We have seen and testify' echoes the LORD's appointment of Israel as witnesses ('you are my witnesses... that I am God'). The covenantal vocation to testify to the one God shapes John's testimony that the Father sent the Son as Savior of the world.

echoes.text: Declare and present it. Yes, let them take counsel together. Who has shown this from ancient time? Who has declared it of old? Haven’t I, Yahweh? There is no other God besides me, a just God and a Savior; There is no one besides me. “Look to me, and be saved, all the ends of the earth; for I am God, and there is no other.
echoes.note: 'The Savior of the world' draws on Isaiah's proclamation of the LORD as the only righteous God and Savior, to whom all the ends of the earth are summoned. John extends this universal salvific scope to the Son sent by the Father.

pericopes.text: In this love has been made perfect among us, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment, because as he is, even so are we in this world. There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment. He who fears is not made perfect in love. We love him, because he first loved us. If a man says, “I love God,” and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who doesn’t love his brother whom he has seen, how can he love God whom he has not seen? This commandment we have from him, that he who loves God should also love his brother.

echoes.text: The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge; but the foolish despise wisdom and instruction.
echoes.note: 'There is no fear in love; perfect love casts out fear' stands in deliberate tension with the wisdom maxim that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge. John transforms the servile fear of judgment into the boldness of perfected love, a development of the biblical fear-of-God tradition.

echoes.text: For wickedness, condemned by a witness within, is a coward thing, And, being pressed hard by conscience, always forecasts the worst lot: For fear is nothing else but a surrender of the help which reason offers;
echoes.note: 'For fear is nothing but a surrender of the helps that come from reason' provides a deuterocanonical reflection on fear as torment and bondage, paralleling John's 'fear has punishment.' The depiction of fear as inner anguish anticipating judgment resonates with John's contrast of fear and perfected love.

echoes.text: Yahweh didn’t set his love on you, nor choose you, because you were more in number than any people; for you were the fewest of all peoples: but because Yahweh loves you, and because he desires to keep the oath which he swore to your fathers, Yahweh has brought you out with a mighty hand, and redeemed you out of the house of bondage, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt.
echoes.note: 'We love him, because he first loved us' restates the Deuteronomic priority of divine election-love that precedes and grounds any human love for God. The prevenient love of the LORD setting his affection on Israel before any response is the template for John's 'he first loved us.'

echoes.text: “‘You shall not hate your brother in your heart. You shall surely rebuke your neighbor, and not bear sin because of him. “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: The charge against one who says 'I love God' yet hates his brother draws on the Holiness Code: 'you shall not hate your brother in your heart... you shall love your neighbor as yourself.' John binds love of God inseparably to love of the visible brother, fulfilling the neighbor command.

echoes.text: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
echoes.note: 'He who loves God should also love his brother' joins the Shema's command to love God with the whole heart to neighbor-love as a single commandment 'we have from him.' John reads the love of God of the Shema as inseparable from the love of brother required by the Holiness Code.

echoes.text: I said in my haste, “All men are liars.”
echoes.note: 'He is a liar' echoes the psalmist's 'all men are liars,' supplying the biblical category of the lie as a failure of covenant truthfulness. The brother-hater who claims love of God is exposed as a liar in the Johannine sense of one who does not do the truth.

echoes.text: “Thus has Yahweh of Armies spoken, saying, ‘Execute true judgment, and show kindness and compassion every man to his brother. Don’t oppress the widow, nor the fatherless, the foreigner, nor the poor; and let none of you devise evil against his brother in your heart.’
echoes.note: The prophetic insistence that true devotion to God is shown by mercy and not oppressing the brother resonates with John's argument that love of the unseen God must be embodied in love of the seen brother. Marked faint as a thematic rather than verbal parallel.

pericopes.text: Whoever believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God. Whoever loves the Father also loves the child who is born of him. By this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God and keep his commandments. For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. His commandments are not grievous. For whatever is born of God overcomes the world. This is the victory that has overcome the world: your faith. Who is he who overcomes the world, but he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?

echoes.text: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
echoes.note: The Shema's command to love God with the whole self stands behind 'when we love God and keep his commandments.' John makes love of God inseparable from obedience, exactly the link Deuteronomy forges. Loving God and keeping commandments are presented as a single covenantal disposition.

echoes.text: For this commandment which I command you this day is not too hard for you or too distant.
echoes.note: 'His commandments are not grievous' closely echoes Moses' insistence that 'this commandment which I command you this day is not too hard for you, neither is it far off.' Both texts answer an anticipated objection that God's law is an unbearable weight. The shared logic is that those rightly related to God find his demands livable, not crushing.

echoes.text: Know therefore that Yahweh your God himself is God, the faithful God, who keeps covenant and loving kindness with them who love him and keep his commandments to a thousand generations,
echoes.note: The pairing of loving God with keeping his commandments matches the covenant formula describing God's faithfulness to 'them that love him and keep his commandments.' John inverts the perspective to the believer's side but preserves the same Deuteronomic word-pair. The covenantal idiom of love-plus-obedience is distinctively Mosaic.

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your seed, to love Yahweh your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, that you may live.
echoes.note: The promise that God will 'circumcise your heart... to love the LORD your God' anticipates John's notion that the one born of God both believes and loves. The new birth that produces obedient love develops the Deuteronomic hope of an inwardly transformed, God-loving heart. Both locate the capacity to love God in a divine act upon the person.

echoes.text: Sing to Yahweh a new song, for he has done marvelous things! His right hand, and his holy arm, have worked salvation for him.
echoes.note: 'This is the victory that has overcome the world' draws on the psalmic celebration that God's 'right hand and his holy arm hath gotten him the victory.' The vocabulary of decisive divine victory is transferred to faith's triumph over the world. The believer shares in a conquest that is ultimately God's own.

echoes.text: For they didn’t get the land in possession by their own sword, neither did their own arm save them; but your right hand, and your arm, and the light of your face, because you were favorable to them.
echoes.note: The motif that victory comes 'not by their own sword' but by God's arm and favor underlies John's claim that the overcoming power is faith rather than human strength. The world is conquered by a God-given means, not by force. The echo is faint and thematic.

echoes.text: I will delight myself in your commandments, because I love them.
echoes.note: The psalmist's delight in commandments he loves complements John's claim that God's commandments 'are not grievous.' Both portray the law as an object of love rather than burden. The connection is conceptual, supporting the un-burdensome framing of obedience.

echoes.text: My son, don’t forget my teaching; but let your heart keep my commandments:
echoes.note: The wisdom appeal to keep the father's commandments in the heart parallels John's keeping-commandments-as-love. Proverbs frames obedience as life-giving rather than oppressive. A faint sapiential backdrop to John's gentle yoke.

pericopes.text: This is he who came by water and blood, Jesus Christ; not with the water only, but with the water and the blood. It is the Spirit who testifies, because the Spirit is the truth. For there are three who testify: the Spirit, the water, and the blood; and the three agree as one. If we receive the witness of men, the witness of God is greater; for this is God’s testimony which he has testified concerning his Son. He who believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself. He who doesn’t believe God has made him a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that God has given concerning his Son. The testimony is this, that God gave to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. He who has the Son has the life. He who doesn’t have God’s Son doesn’t have the life.

echoes.text: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sins. At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall a matter be established.
echoes.note: 'There are three who testify... and the three agree as one' applies the Mosaic rule that a matter is established 'at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses.' John assembles exactly the legally sufficient number of corroborating witnesses to validate the testimony about the Son. The juridical framework of accredited witnesses is drawn straight from the Torah's evidentiary law.

echoes.text: At the mouth of two witnesses, or three witnesses, he who is to die shall be put to death. At the mouth of one witness he shall not be put to death.
echoes.note: The companion legal principle requiring multiple witnesses to establish a capital matter reinforces John's threefold testimony. The Spirit, water, and blood function as the plurality of witnesses that secures conviction in God's case for his Son. The forensic logic of confirmed testimony is Deuteronomic.

echoes.text: “‘Whoever kills any person, the murderer shall be slain at the mouth of witnesses; but one witness shall not testify against any person that he die.
echoes.note: The legal insistence that no single witness suffices, but a plurality establishes the verdict, undergirds John's grouping of three concurring witnesses. The motif that life-and-death matters demand corroborated testimony fits John's life-giving testimony about the Son. A further Pentateuchal source for the witness-rule.

echoes.text: For the life of the flesh is in the blood; and I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that makes atonement by reason of the life.
echoes.note: The blood among the witnesses evokes the Levitical principle that 'the life of the flesh is in the blood' and that blood makes atonement. John's 'water and blood' draws atoning significance from the sacrificial system where blood is the witnessing, life-bearing agent. The blood testifies because it is the locus of atoning life.

echoes.text: He shall take some of the blood of the bull, and sprinkle it with his finger on the mercy seat on the east; and before the mercy seat he shall sprinkle some of the blood with his finger seven times.
echoes.note: The Day of Atonement sprinkling of blood stands behind the atoning weight John gives 'the blood.' The cleansing blood ritual informs the salvific testimony of Christ's blood. A faint cultic resonance underlying the witness of blood.

echoes.text: “A man who is clean shall gather up the ashes of the heifer, and lay them up outside of the camp in a clean place; and it shall be kept for the congregation of the children of Israel for a water for impurity. It is a sin offering.
echoes.note: The 'water of purification' from the red heifer informs the cleansing connotation of 'the water' among the witnesses. Purifying water and atoning blood together echo the Pentateuchal rites of cleansing. The pairing of water and blood recalls Israel's purification system.

echoes.text: Moses took half of the blood and put it in basins, and half of the blood he sprinkled on the altar. He took the book of the covenant and read it in the hearing of the people, and they said, “All that Yahweh has spoken will we do, and be obedient.” Moses took the blood, and sprinkled it on the people, and said, “Look, this is the blood of the covenant, which Yahweh has made with you concerning all these words.”
echoes.note: The covenant ratification in which Moses applies the blood and the people pledge obedience associates blood with sealed testimony. John's blood-witness to the Son parallels the blood that confirmed the covenant. A faint covenantal-blood backdrop to the witnessing blood.

echoes.text: “You are my witnesses,” says Yahweh, “With my servant whom I have chosen; that you may know and believe me, and understand that I am he. Before me there was no God formed, neither will there be after me.
echoes.note: God's declaration 'Ye are my witnesses... that ye may know and believe me' parallels John's structure of divine testimony aimed at belief and knowledge of God. The 'testimony of God' that one must receive develops Isaiah's courtroom scenes where God testifies to himself. Both stage a trial in which God's own witness compels faith.

echoes.text: Turn your ear, and come to me; hear, and your soul shall live: and I will make an everlasting covenant with you, even the sure mercies of David.
echoes.note: The offer of 'an everlasting covenant... the sure mercies of David' and the call to 'hear, and your soul shall live' resonate with John's 'God gave to us eternal life.' Hearing God's testimony issues in life. A faint resonance for life granted through receiving God's word.

echoes.text: For whoever finds me, finds life, and will obtain favor from Yahweh.
echoes.note: Wisdom's promise 'whoso findeth me findeth life' parallels 'He who has the Son has the life.' Possessing the divine gift is possessing life itself. A sapiential echo for life located in a person to be found.

echoes.text: For wisdom is a spirit that loves man, And she will not hold a blasphemer guiltless for his lips; Because God bears witness of his reins, And is a true overseer of his heart, And a hearer of his tongue:
echoes.note: The portrayal of the Spirit as a witness who searches and testifies of inward truth resonates with 'It is the Spirit who testifies, because the Spirit is the truth.' The deuterocanonical conception of the Spirit as truthful witness anticipates John's Spirit-testimony. The connection is thematic and faint.

pericopes.text: These things I have written to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life, and that you may continue to believe in the name of the Son of God. echoes.text: Yahweh is near to all those who call on him, to all who call on him in truth. He will fulfill the desire of those who fear him. He also will hear their cry, and will save them.
echoes.note: 'If we ask anything according to his will, he listens to us' echoes the psalm that 'the LORD is nigh unto all them that call upon him... he will hear their cry, and will save them.' Both ground confident prayer in God's reliable hearing of those rightly disposed toward him. The assurance that petitions are heard is psalmic.

echoes.text: “‘But the soul who does anything with a high hand, whether he is native-born or a foreigner, the same blasphemes Yahweh. That soul shall be cut off from among his people. Because he has despised Yahweh’s word, and has broken his commandment, that soul shall utterly be cut off. His iniquity shall be on him.’”
echoes.note: The 'sin leading to death,' for which intercession is withheld, draws on the Torah's distinction between unintentional sin (atonable) and the 'high-handed' sin that 'reproacheth the LORD,' whose soul 'shall be utterly cut off.' John's two-tier sin scheme mirrors the Pentateuchal contrast between forgivable error and defiant apostasy that forfeits atonement. The deadly sin is the presumptuous, deliberate rejection that excludes from the covenant.

echoes.text: If one man sin against another, God shall judge him; but if a man sin against Yahweh, who shall entreat for him?” Notwithstanding, they didn’t listen to the voice of their father, because Yahweh intended to kill them.
echoes.note: Eli's words, 'if a man sin against the LORD, who shall intreat for him?'—spoken of sons whom the LORD willed to slay—anticipate the sin for which John says one should not pray. Both mark a sin so grave that intercession is futile or inappropriate. The notion of a sin beyond the reach of petition is shared.

echoes.text: “Therefore don’t pray for this people, neither lift up a cry nor prayer for them, neither make intercession to me; for I will not hear you.
echoes.note: God's command to Jeremiah, 'pray not thou for this people... for I will not hear thee,' parallels John's 'I don't say that he should make a request concerning this.' Both texts identify a condition of sin under which intercession is forbidden or pointless. The withholding of prayer for the hardened sinner is a prophetic precedent.

echoes.text: “‘If one person sins unwittingly, then he shall offer a female goat a year old for a sin offering. The priest shall make atonement for the soul who errs, when he sins unwittingly before Yahweh, to make atonement for him; and he shall be forgiven.
echoes.note: The provision of atonement for the soul that 'sinneth through ignorance' corresponds to John's 'sin not leading to death,' for which one may pray and receive life. The forgivable, unintentional category in the Torah underlies John's lesser sin. The two-fold sin distinction is rooted in sacrificial law.

echoes.text: Now therefore, take to yourselves seven bulls and seven rams, and go to my servant Job, and offer up for yourselves a burnt offering; and my servant Job shall pray for you, for I will accept him, that I not deal with you according to your folly. For you have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job has.”
echoes.note: God's instruction that Job pray for his friends so they be not dealt with after their folly models intercession granting life to fellow sinners. John's 'he shall ask, and God will give him life' parallels the effective intercession for another's sin. A faint precedent for life secured through a brother's prayer.

echoes.text: Now therefore, restore the man’s wife. For he is a prophet, and he will pray for you, and you will live. If you don’t restore her, know for sure that you will die, you, and all who are yours.”
echoes.note: The promise that Abraham 'shall pray for thee, and thou shalt live' anticipates intercession that restores life to a sinner. John's framework of asking on behalf of a sinning brother to gain him life resonates with this pattern. The link is faint and thematic.

echoes.text: Yahweh of Armies revealed himself in my ears, “Surely this iniquity will not be forgiven you until you die,” says the Lord, Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: The oracle that 'this iniquity shall not be purged from you till ye die' depicts an unpardonable sin terminating in death, paralleling John's 'sin leading to death.' Both envision guilt that atonement cannot reach. A faint prophetic analogue to the deadly sin.

pericopes.text: We know that whoever is born of God doesn’t sin, but he who was born of God keeps himself, and the evil one doesn’t touch him. We know that we are of God, and the whole world lies in the power of the evil one. We know that the Son of God has come, and has given us an understanding, that we know him who is true, and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God, and eternal life. Little children, keep yourselves from idols.

echoes.text: “You shall have no other gods before me. “You shall not make for yourselves an idol, nor any image of anything that is in the heavens above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
echoes.note: 'Keep yourselves from idols' enforces the first and second commandments against having other gods and making graven images. John ends by recalling the Decalogue's foundational prohibition of idolatry as the boundary of covenant loyalty. To 'keep from idols' is to keep the first words of Sinai.

echoes.text: “You shall have no other gods before me. “You shall not make an engraved image for yourself, any likeness of what is in heaven above, or what is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth. You shall not bow yourself down to them, nor serve them; for I, Yahweh, your God, am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, and on the third and on the fourth generation of those who hate me;
echoes.note: The Deuteronomic restatement of the prohibition against other gods and idols stands directly behind John's closing command. The contrast between the 'true God' and lifeless idols mirrors Deuteronomy's exclusive covenant claim. John's farewell is a compressed reaffirmation of the Mosaic anti-idolatry charge.

echoes.text: But Yahweh is the true God; he is the living God, and an everlasting King: at his wrath the earth trembles, and the nations are not able to withstand his indignation.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's contrast that 'the LORD is the true God... the living God' against the worthless idols he has just mocked directly informs John's 'This is the true God' followed by 'keep yourselves from idols.' The polemical pairing of the one true God with the renunciation of idols is shared. John echoes Jeremiah's living-and-true-God formula and its anti-idol thrust.

echoes.text: Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men’s hands. They have mouths, but they don’t speak. They have eyes, but they don’t see. They have ears, but they don’t hear. They have noses, but they don’t smell. They have hands, but they don’t feel. They have feet, but they don’t walk, neither do they speak through their throat. Those who make them will be like them; yes, everyone who trusts in them.
echoes.note: The mockery of idols that are the work of men's hands, who 'have eyes... but they see not,' underlies John's antithesis between the true God and idols. The closing warning assumes the psalmist's verdict on idols as dead and powerless. The 'true God and eternal life' is the living antithesis to lifeless images.

echoes.text: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”
echoes.note: 'The evil one doesn't touch him' and 'the whole world lies in the power of the evil one' presuppose the primeval enmity between the serpent and the offspring of the woman. The one born of God is guarded against the serpent who holds the world. The protology of the serpent-adversary informs John's cosmic dualism.

echoes.text: If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.”
echoes.note: Sin 'lieth at the door' desiring to master Cain, while the called one must rule over it, parallels the one born of God who 'keeps himself' so the evil one cannot touch him. Both portray an external malevolent power kept at bay by the faithful. A faint backdrop to self-keeping against an encroaching evil.

echoes.text: Haven’t you made a hedge around him, and around his house, and around all that he has, on every side? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his substance is increased in the land.
echoes.note: The hedge God set 'about him, and about his house' that the adversary could not breach parallels the one born of God whom 'the evil one doesn't touch.' Divine protection bars the satan's reach in both. A faint analogue for the believer's guarded immunity.

echoes.text: The Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are just. A God of faithfulness who does no wrong, just and right is he.
echoes.note: The Song of Moses naming God 'a God of truth and without iniquity, just and right' resonates with John's 'him who is true' and 'the true God.' The divine attribute of truth/faithfulness is a Pentateuchal predicate. A faint resonance for the God who is true.

echoes.text: so that he who blesses himself in the earth shall bless himself in the God of truth; and he who swears in the earth shall swear by the God of truth; because the former troubles are forgotten, and because they are hidden from my eyes.
echoes.note: Blessing and swearing 'by the God of truth' anticipates John's emphatic 'the true God.' The covenant God defined over against false gods is the God of truth. A faint prophetic precedent for the title.

echoes.text: For the worship of those nameless idols Is a beginning and cause and end of every evil.
echoes.note: The deuterocanonical judgment that 'the worship of idols not to be named is the beginning... and the end of all evil' supports John's coupling of the evil-dominated world with the warning against idols. Idolatry as the root of the world's evil frames John's final exhortation. The connection is thematic and faint.
